You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash

```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Six checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Runs automatically after the
Sunday 02:30 adjudication job.

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" Deck Series (Education_Content_Agent)

The "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" series is a set of short educational decks for Baylor Applied Performance, generated programmatically by the `Education_Content_Agent` project. On 2026-08-19, three alternative visual directions were built as samples, the user selected the "split field" direction, and all five topic decks were rebuilt in it. The selected direction was written into `build-all.js` as the default so a later rebuild cannot silently revert to the prior editorial look.

## Key Points

- **Three directions were built as real samples, not descriptions:** A — *sequence rail* (a five-step argument along the top, current step lit); B — *split field* (a hard vertical divide, claim on dark green and evidence on bone, both visible at once); C — *annotated evidence* (numbered figure plus caption, paper-style). B was recommended and chosen.
- **The chosen direction became the code default.** `build-all.js` now defaults to split field, with `--direction annotated | sequence-rail | editorial` retained as opt-in flags. The stated rationale was explicitly about future-proofing: a rebuild six months later must not quietly produce the old design.
- **Prior versions were preserved, not overwritten.** The user declined the OneDrive overwrite; `5slides5minutes/` on OneDrive was left untouched at 10 decks (5 new topics in the previous design plus ACWR, CMJ, GPS, HRV, VBT), and the previous-design decks were pulled back down to `decks-out/previous-editorial-design/` so they exist in two places rather than only on a synced drive.
- **A PowerPoint-free renderer was built** that reads `.pptx` directly, after PowerPoint automation broke following a force-quit. Its text spacing is approximate in preview; the `.pptx` files themselves remain exact.
- **Layouts authored for full-width slides break in narrow columns.** The two-card comparison layout in the Post-Practice deck had headings wrapping into body text under the split field's narrower column; the fix was to stack the cards when the column is tight.

## Details

The session's structure — build three fully realized directions, view them side by side, then commit one — treats visual direction as a decision to be made against rendered artifacts rather than against prose descriptions. The three samples plus a `compare.html` contact sheet live in `decks-out/variants/`, which means the rejected directions remain inspectable rather than being discarded with the decision. This matters because the three directions encode genuinely different rhetorical structures: the sequence rail foregrounds a stepwise argument, the annotated-evidence direction foregrounds the figure as the primary object, and the split field holds claim and evidence in simultaneous view. Choosing among them is a choice about how the five-minute talk argues, not merely how it looks.

Encoding the chosen direction as the `build-all.js` default is the durability half of the decision. A generated-artifact pipeline whose visual direction lives only in the invocation flags will regress to whatever the code's default happens to be the next time someone runs a rebuild without remembering the flag — and the person running it six months out may not know a choice was ever made. Writing the selection into the default converts an undocumented convention into a property of the build, while the `--direction` flags keep the alternatives reachable. The parallel preservation decision applies the same reasoning to outputs: rather than overwriting the OneDrive copies, the previous-design decks were pulled back down into a named local archive folder, so the prior versions survive in a second location that does not depend on a synced cloud drive remaining intact.

The split field's narrower content column exposed a latent assumption in the deck layouts. The two-card comparison layout in the Post-Practice deck had been authored against a full-width slide and, once constrained, produced headings that wrapped into their own body text. The general lesson is that layouts inherit an unstated width assumption from the design they were first authored under, and a design-direction change is effectively a viewport change for every layout in the corpus — the same class of defect as slide charts that overflow only at short landscape viewports in [[concepts/athlete-monitoring-rtp-presentation]]. The fix, stacking the cards when the column is tight, is a responsive rule rather than a per-slide patch.

# Automated Layout QA Gate for Generated Decks

The layout QA gate is an automated pre-review check in the `Education_Content_Agent` deck pipeline that inspects generated slides for layout defects before a human looks at them. On the 2026-08-19 deck rebuild it caught 8 layout bugs across three direction variants and reported 491 passing checks on the final five-deck build. The session also established the gate's two documented blind spots: it detects box-versus-box collisions but cannot detect text overflowing its own box, and it misread split-layout slides until taught about them.

## Key Points

- **What it catches:** box-versus-box collisions between slide elements. This is a geometric check on element bounding boxes and is reliable within that scope.
- **What it cannot catch:** text overflowing *its own* box. The container's geometry is unchanged when its text spills, so a collision check sees nothing wrong — exactly the defect class that produced the narrow-column heading-into-body-text bug in the Post-Practice deck.
- **False positives from unmodeled layouts:** the gate misread split-layout slides because it could not tell which side of the divide text sat on, generating false positives until it was taught about split layouts. A checker that does not model a layout type will report confidently and wrongly about it.
- **Scale of value:** 8 layout bugs caught pre-review across three variants; 491 checks passed on the final build. The gate's worth is in the volume of mechanical verification it removes from human review, not in completeness.
- **Supporting render path:** `cairosvg` fails on this machine (missing native library), so the working substitute was an HTML contact sheet viewed in Chrome. A PowerPoint-free renderer reading `.pptx` directly was built after PowerPoint automation broke; its preview text spacing is approximate while the `.pptx` files remain exact.

## Details

The gate's blind spots are more instructive than its coverage, because both are failures of *scope* rather than of implementation. Box-versus-box collision detection answers a narrower question than "is this slide laid out correctly": it asks whether two elements overlap, and text spilling past its own container's bounds does not change that container's geometry at all. So the single most common generated-deck defect — content too long for the space allotted — sits precisely in the gate's gap. This is the same shape as a status field that reports accurately on a narrower predicate than the operational question, catalogued in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]]: the check is not lying, it is answering a different question than the one being asked of it.

The split-layout false positives are the complementary failure. Because the gate had no model of a hard vertical divide, it could not determine which side of the divide a text element belonged to, and so reported collisions that were not real. An automated checker applied to a layout family it does not model does not fail silently or abstain — it emits confident wrong answers, which is worse than no check, because false positives train the reader to discount the gate's output. Teaching the gate about split layouts was therefore not a nicety but a precondition for the direction change being verifiable at all.

Several supporting-tooling failures in the same session reinforce that the verification path itself must be watched. `cairosvg` could not run for lack of a native library, and the substitute was an HTML contact sheet rendered in Chrome — a lower-tech but working viewport. Silenced or backgrounded regeneration steps hid a failure and served stale SVGs, so regeneration was moved back to running visibly; an edit that stopped `deck_preview` from writing individual SVGs caused the comparison page to read first-run files until it was restored; and `build-all.js` was globbing and executing `build-variants.js` until the glob filter was fixed. Each of these produced output that looked plausible while being stale or wrong, which is the reason the visible-regeneration rule was adopted. Together with the approximate text spacing in the PowerPoint-free preview — accurate enough to judge layout, not accurate enough to judge exact spacing — the session's practical rule is that the gate is a filter that removes mechanical defects before human review, not a substitute for looking at the rendered artifact.

# Connection: Archive the Prior Version Before a Restyle, in a Second Location

## The Connection

Three separate deck efforts arrive at the same discipline from different directions. On 2026-08-19 the user declined an OneDrive overwrite of the "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" decks, leaving the 10 existing decks untouched and having the previous-design versions pulled back down to a local `decks-out/previous-editorial-design/` folder — explicitly so they exist in two places rather than only on a synced drive. On 2026-06-18 the 11-slide RTP conference deck was reconstructed from git and preserved as `RTP-Data-Collection-v1.html` before the 14-slide v2 replaced it as the working file ([[concepts/athlete-monitoring-rtp-presentation]]). On 2026-07-09 the merged clinic deck was saved as `UPDATED_Clinic_Presentation_v2.pptx` at the user's explicit request, leaving the original untouched ([[concepts/baylor-performance-clinic-presentation]]).

## Key Insight

A restyle is not an edit — it is a *replacement* of an artifact that a human already judged acceptable, and the judgment is not recoverable from the new version. Regenerating the old look from a `--direction editorial` flag would produce something similar but not the thing that was previously reviewed and shipped, so the old build must be kept as an artifact rather than as a reproducible recipe.

The 2026-08-19 case adds a constraint the other two do not state: **the archive must live somewhere other than the synced drive.** Pulling the previous decks *down* from OneDrive into a local folder was the operative move, because a copy that exists only on a cloud-synced drive shares a failure mode with the thing it is meant to protect — a sync error, an accidental overwrite from another machine, or a folder-level replace takes both. The same reasoning drives the "exists in two places" framing in [[concepts/crashbox-ssd-backup-baseline]] and the fail-closed manifest in [[concepts/dev-folder-manifest-default-deny]]: the value of a backup is a function of how independent its failure mode is from the original's.

The corollary for delivery is that new versions go out under *new filenames*. The open action item from 2026-08-19 — add the split-field decks to OneDrive under different filenames, never replacing the previous ones — makes the two generations coexist for their audience rather than forcing a cutover, which is the same reason the clinic deck shipped as `_v2` alongside an untouched original.

# Run Regeneration Visibly: Silenced Build Steps Serve Stale Artifacts

A regeneration step whose output is silenced or backgrounded can fail without announcing it, after which every downstream consumer reads the previous run's artifacts and reports success. On 2026-08-19, three variants of this failure appeared in a single deck-build session, and the operating rule adopted was to run regeneration visibly rather than quietly.

## Key Points

- **Silenced/backgrounded regeneration hid a failure and served stale SVGs.** Nothing errored visibly; consumers simply read the prior run's files. The fix was procedural — run regeneration where its output is seen.
- **A code edit silently removed an output.** An edit that stopped `deck_preview` from writing individual SVGs caused the comparison page to fall back to reading first-run files; the write was restored. Removing an artifact-producing side effect is invisible when a stale copy of that artifact still exists on disk.
- **A glob matched more than intended.** `build-all.js` was globbing and executing `build-variants.js`; the filter was fixed. Pattern-based file selection silently widens as sibling files accumulate.
- **The common signature is a successful-looking run over old inputs** — the same shape as a graph artifact built before its newest extraction layer existed, and as a backup manifest that omits folders while every step reports OK.
- **Stale artifacts are worse than missing ones,** because a missing file surfaces as an error at the consumer while a stale file surfaces as nothing at all.

## Details

All three failures in this session share a structure: a step that was supposed to produce fresh output did not, and because a previous run's output was still present on disk, the pipeline continued and produced a plausible result. Backgrounding or silencing a step removes the only channel through which its failure would have been noticed, so the choice to run a build step quietly is not merely a cosmetic preference — it converts a loud failure into a silent one whenever stale outputs exist. The same reasoning applies to the `deck_preview` edit: dropping the individual-SVG write was a change with no immediate symptom precisely because the files it used to write were already there from the first run.

The glob case adds a second lesson about implicit scope. `build-all.js` selected scripts by pattern and thereby picked up `build-variants.js`, executing a sibling that was never meant to be part of that run. Pattern-based selection encodes an assumption about which files will exist in a directory, and that assumption silently weakens every time a new file is added next to the matched ones — the build's behavior changes without the build being edited. The corrective is an explicit filter, which is the same move as replacing an inferred boundary with a declared one in [[connections/git-repository-boundaries-should-be-explicit]].

The generalizable rule is that a pipeline's freshness cannot be inferred from its exit codes when its stages write to a shared, persistent output directory. Either each stage must be observed as it runs, or the consumer must verify that the artifacts it reads were produced by the current run — for example by rebuilding downstream artifacts unconditionally after every upstream pass, the discipline arrived at independently in the graph-refresh work. In the deck session the chosen remedy was the cheaper one: make the steps visible, so a failure is seen when it happens rather than inferred later from a wrong-looking artifact.

# Connection: Encode the Choice as the Default, Not as a Remembered Flag

## The Connection

When the split-field direction was chosen for the "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" decks on 2026-08-19, the stated reason for writing it into `build-all.js` as the default — rather than simply passing `--direction split-field` on future rebuilds — was that a rebuild six months later must not silently revert to the old editorial look. The alternatives were kept reachable as explicit flags, but the *unflagged* behavior was changed to match the decision.

This is the same structural move as the `~/DEV` backup manifest failing closed on unlisted folders in [[concepts/dev-folder-manifest-default-deny]]. In both cases a decision that could have lived in a human's memory or in an invocation habit was instead relocated into the system's behavior when nobody is paying attention.

## Key Insight

**The default is the decision that actually gets made.** A flag encodes what someone remembers to type; the default encodes what happens when they do not. Any choice preserved only as a flag has an expiry date set by human memory, and its silent reversal produces output that looks finished and correct while embodying the rejected option.

The two cases sit on opposite ends of the same axis, which is what makes the pairing informative:

- **Default-to-the-decision (deck build):** the default *is* the chosen behavior, so forgetting the flag is harmless. Appropriate where one option is right and the others are occasional.
- **Default-to-refusal (backup manifest):** the default is to fail rather than to guess, so an unclassified input halts instead of being silently included or excluded. Appropriate where the right answer depends on information the system does not have — and it caught a real omission within a minute of being installed.

The selection rule between them is whether the system can know the correct answer without asking. When it can, bake the answer in. When it cannot, bake in the refusal — never a guess. What is never acceptable is a default that silently supplies the *previously* correct answer, which is what the editorial direction would have been six months on.

## Evidence

- 2026-08-19: "**Split field (B) is now the default direction** in `build-all.js`, so a rebuild six months from now can't silently revert to the old editorial look. Other directions remain available via `--direction annotated | sequence-rail | editorial`."
- 2026-09-01 ([[concepts/dev-folder-manifest-default-deny]]): the backup manifest was changed to fail closed on any unlisted `~/DEV` folder, and caught an unlisted folder within a minute — the omission class that per-stage success reporting cannot see.
- The contrast with [[concepts/five-slides-five-minutes-deck-series]]' sibling decision is instructive: the *previous* deck versions were preserved by explicit archival to `decks-out/previous-editorial-design/`, because preservation of an artifact cannot be encoded as a default in the same way a build behavior can — it required a positive action.

# PowerPoint-Free .pptx Renderer as an Automation Fallback

After PowerPoint automation broke following a force-quit, a renderer was built on 2026-08-19 that reads `.pptx` files directly rather than driving the PowerPoint application. It restored the ability to preview generated decks without the host application, at the cost of approximate text spacing — the `.pptx` files themselves remain exact, and only the preview is an approximation.

## Key Points

- **Trigger:** force-quitting PowerPoint left its automation interface broken, removing the render path the deck pipeline depended on. The response was to replace the dependency rather than repair the application state.
- **Approach:** read the `.pptx` format directly and render from it, eliminating the host-application dependency entirely for preview purposes.
- **Known fidelity limit:** text spacing in the preview is approximate. This is accurate enough to judge layout and composition but not exact spacing — a limitation that must be stated whenever the preview is used as evidence.
- **The exact artifact is unchanged.** Only the preview is approximate; the delivered `.pptx` files are authoritative and unaffected by the renderer's fidelity.
- **A parallel fallback in the same session:** `cairosvg` failed for a missing native library, and an HTML contact sheet viewed in Chrome served as the working substitute for visual comparison.

## Details

Both fallbacks in this session follow the same move: when a rendering dependency is unavailable — a broken automation interface in one case, a missing native library in the other — substitute a path that reads the artifact more directly rather than trying to restore the broken layer. Reading `.pptx` directly removes an entire class of failure (application state, automation permissions, force-quit residue) from the preview path, and rendering an HTML contact sheet in a browser removes the native-library dependency that `cairosvg` required. In both cases the substitute is lower-fidelity but more robust, and in both cases the substitute was adequate because the question being asked of the preview was compositional rather than typographic.

The fidelity caveat is what makes the fallback usable rather than dangerous. A preview that is approximate but *known* to be approximate can be relied on for the judgments it supports and distrusted for the ones it does not; an unlabeled approximation invites conclusions the render cannot support. The specific boundary here — layout and element placement are judgeable, exact text spacing is not — matters directly for the deck QA work in the same session, since the gate's documented blind spot is text overflowing its own box, and an approximate-spacing preview is precisely the wrong instrument for confirming or refuting that class of defect. The authoritative artifact remains the `.pptx` file itself, so any spacing question must be settled by opening the real file rather than the preview.

# SportScienceResearchRepo Batch PDF Import Pipeline

SportScienceResearchRepo maintains a `papers.json` database of sports-science research papers, built up through an ongoing batch-import campaign that processes a large backlog of football-related PDFs in rounds. On 2026-04-21, round 7 used 10 parallel subagents to add papers with IDs 334-383 to the database. A follow-up session on 2026-04-22 resolved a set of `year: 0`/blank-data quality issues left over from earlier rounds, including two that round 7 itself had flagged.

## Key Points

- Each import round assigns a contiguous block of IDs (round 7: 334-383, 50 papers) across 10 parallel subagents, with each agent handling a 5-paper batch.
- Before writing agent prompts for a new round, the format/schema is confirmed against a recently-completed batch file to keep entries consistent across rounds.
- Agents complete in non-sequential order; completions are tracked individually (round 7: agents 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 finished first, with agents 4, 6, and 10 still outstanding) before a separate "merge agent" consolidates all 10 batch files into `papers.json` and pushes the result.
- The `papers.json` schema includes a `"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE"` marker for entries whose source PDF cannot be located on disk, used for ID 358 (a KIAA0319 genetics paper) until it was resolved on 2026-04-22.
- On 2026-04-22, a repair session fixed 6 entries with `year: 0`/blank data carried over from earlier rounds: IDs 286 and 287 (true duplicates), 292 and 294 (unreadable filenames), 336 (a misassigned URL, recataloged from an ankle-sprain paper to Xia et al. 2024 on gut microbiota), and 358 (the KIAA0319 paper, originally blocked by non-breaking spaces in its filename) - resolving both of the data-quality issues round 7 had flagged (336 and 358).
- A background repair agent's proposed fixes (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`) contained hallucinated author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358; these were corrected via PyPDF2 text extraction directly from the source PDFs before committing, and round 8 was set to begin at ID 384 (~319 papers remaining across rounds 8-12).

## Details

The batch-import campaign works through a large backlog of football-related research PDFs in fixed-size rounds, each adding 50 papers via 10 parallel 5-paper agent batches. This parallelization lets a round's worth of extraction work happen concurrently, but it also means completion tracking has to happen at the individual-agent level - in round 7, seven of the ten agents (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9) finished before the remaining three (4, 6, 10), and the round could not be merged until all ten reported done. Once all batch files are complete, a dedicated merge agent consolidates them into the shared `papers.json` and pushes the update, advancing the repo's paper count (333 -> 383 after round 7).

Round 7 also surfaced several data-quality edge cases that the pipeline has conventions for handling rather than blocking on. ID 358 could not be matched to any PDF on disk and was marked `"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE"` per schema rather than skipped entirely. ID 336's source PDF had a curly apostrophe in its filename (URL-encoded as `%E2%80%99` in its `driveUrl`), which prevented the file from being read - this was logged as an open issue to investigate and fix rather than resolved inline. ID 343's PDF was misnamed "NFL Play Smart" but actually contained an unrelated hamstring-injury paper (Vermeulen et al.), requiring the agent to catalog it under its true content rather than its filename. ID 340 (Dupont et al., on lumbar disk herniation) used a Wolters Kluwer "in-press" DOI format whose final form was uncertain, so it was flagged for staff verification rather than guessed at. Together these conventions - explicit "unreadable" markers, content-based (not filename-based) cataloging, and flagging-for-review rather than guessing - keep the dataset complete and auditable even when individual source files are problematic.

The 2026-04-22 session closed out exactly the two issues round 7 had flagged - ID 358 (unreadable filename) and ID 336 (curly-apostrophe filename/misassigned URL) - alongside four additional `year: 0`/blank entries (286, 287, 292, 294) discovered separately. The session began by discovering that a previous session's background repair agent, which had produced a candidate fix file (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`), had not actually finished its work - so the fix was resumed from scratch rather than assumed complete. Worse, where the agent HAD produced output, its proposed citations for IDs 286, 287, and 358 had hallucinated author lists despite identifying the correct paper topics; for ID 336, the agent had also proposed the wrong replacement paper entirely (an ankle-sprain study) before the correct one (Xia et al. 2024, on gut microbiota) was identified. All three hallucinated citations were caught and corrected by extracting the actual text of the source PDFs with PyPDF2 (run via Bash) and re-citing from that verified text. The session also confirmed that non-breaking spaces and curly apostrophes embedded in PDF filenames - the root cause of IDs 358 and 336's original "unreadable" status - break Claude Code's `Read` tool, and that the practical workaround is PyPDF2 text extraction via Bash combined with exact byte-level filename inspection rather than retyping filenames by hand. A durable procedural lesson also emerged: always verify that a previous session's background agents actually completed before assuming their work is done, since the r7 repair agent had left its fix file incomplete.

# Athlete Monitoring / Return-to-Play Conference Presentation Design

On 2026-06-17, a conference presentation slide deck (~20-min talk) was designed for a visually-oriented sports science audience covering athlete monitoring and return-to-play data workflows. The design process resolved four key architectural decisions — framing, statistical thresholds, content constraints, and audience philosophy — and produced a locked 11-slide running order built around a single-athlete RTP narrative with minimal text and strong visual anchors. A subsequent validation pass confirmed all slides were layout-clean and fixed a dark-mode visibility bug on the final slide. On 2026-06-18, a full speaker script was written for the deck (`RTP-Data-Collection-SCRIPT.md`), a duration analysis showed the 11-slide deck ran far short of its 20-minute slot, and the deck was expanded to 14 slides (v2) with v1 preserved.

## Key Points

- **Single-athlete framing throughout:** roster-comparison views were explicitly rejected as "off-topic for the individual RTP framing." The presentation's decision-support narrative only holds together when the audience follows one athlete's trajectory from injury through return-to-competition decisions. Adding a roster view introduces a different clinical use case that fragments narrative coherence.
- **Visual-first audience philosophy:** the intended audience "eats with their eyes" — conversational delivery carries the explanatory load while slides provide visual anchors, not text. Minimal text per slide; strong imagery and color-coded indicators are the design primitives.
- **Z-score traffic-light thresholds: −1.5 SD / −2 SD.** Applied in the Excel demo to translate raw metrics into actionable status flags. −1.5 SD = caution/yellow; −2 SD = concern/red. The leave-behind template implements the same logic, ensuring the presentation and the artifact practitioners actually use share the same statistical foundation.
- **Screenshots-only (no live build):** consistent with the leave-behind template format. All data visualization examples appear as screenshots rather than live-built charts, eliminating technical failure risk in a conference setting.
- **11-slide running order:** bridge → decision-first framing (×2) → generalizing → metric selection → blank template → populated/flagged → charted → stakeholder report → take-home materials → close.
- **Slide 9 — Sample Stakeholder Report:** single-athlete trend chart + color-coded status flag + one plain-language interpretive line. Models the exact artifact the audience would produce and deliver to coaching/medical staff, completing the "here is the workflow" → "here is the output" arc.
- **Josse referenced verbally only (not on-screen):** a named methodological reference was kept off slides for sensitivity reasons; verbal attribution suffices for academic credentialing without creating a circulating visual artifact.
- **Slide validation (Session 23:56):** All 11 slides confirmed layout-clean at 1440×900 and 375×667. Synthetic keyboard event dispatch (`keydown`) is unreliable for slide navigation in browser automation — smooth-scroll does not complete on synthetic key events in browser extension automation contexts. Use direct navigation-dot element clicks for reliable automated HTML slide deck validation.
- **Dark-background slides require adaptive nav chrome:** Slide 11 uses a dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`); the default nav-dot and slide-counter colors (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`) are invisible against it. Fix: an `on-dark` CSS class toggled on `<body>` by the `setActive()` JavaScript function enables CSS overrides for nav elements on dark slides. This pattern generalizes to any HTML slide deck with alternating light/dark slide backgrounds.
- **A tight, purposeful deck runs far shorter than its slot (2026-06-18):** the 11-slide "You Have the Data. Now What?" deck at correct density runs ~5–7 minutes (7–9 with pauses), leaving an 11–14 minute gap against the 20-minute target. Closing the gap requires real content (case-study athlete walkthrough, live-demo narration for the data table and chart slides, planted audience Q&A), not padding — slide count and density are the drivers, not verbosity.
- **Speaker script + v1/v2 versioning (2026-06-18):** a full per-slide speaker script with talking points, notes, and pacing was saved to `outputs/presentation/RTP-Data-Collection-SCRIPT.md`. # Connection: Silent Omission Defeats Per-Stage Success

## The Connection

Three findings across two consecutive days share a shape that ordinary error handling cannot catch. On 2026-09-01 the `~/DEV` graph was shipped with 0 of 256 Gemini nodes present — not because the merge code was wrong, but because the graph was built at 20:55 against a layer written at 01:22, so the merge was never re-run. In the same session, a scope filter dropped all 130 converted office documents, because the conversion step wrote `.md` files *into* a folder the extractor excluded. On 2026-08-31 the daily backup failed because three project folders were absent from a hand-maintained manifest. In every case each individual stage executed successfully and reported success; the defect lives entirely in what was never presented to the next stage.

## Key Insight

Per-stage success does not compose into artifact correctness, because a stage can only report on the inputs it received. A merge that merges everything it was given is correct; a backup that backs up every path in its manifest is correct; an extractor that skips an excluded folder is correct. None of them can detect that the input set itself was wrong, since "what should have been here" is not available at the stage boundary. Error handling, exit codes, and status fields are all scoped to execution and are therefore structurally blind to omission.

Two remedies appear in these cases, and they are not interchangeable. The first is **fail-closed on unlisted input**: the backup manifest's default-deny turns an omission into a visible `backup-error` within a minute, which is why the 2026-08-31 gap was caught at all rather than producing a quietly smaller backup. The second is **verify the artifact against an independent expectation**: nothing in the graph pipeline could have failed closed on the stale layer, because the merge had no way to know a newer layer existed — it took Codex reading the finished artifact and asking "are these 256 nodes here?" to surface it. The choice between them depends on whether the omission is detectable at the boundary (use a guard) or only in the output (use an independent check). The general rule that follows is the operational one the graph session adopted: rebuild the artifact after every input change and re-verify the artifact itself, rather than trusting that green stages imply a correct result.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-01 (20:31): "Shipped a graph built at 20:55 with a Gemini layer written at 01:22 — 0 of 256 Gemini nodes were present. Merge code was correct; it just was never re-run." The resulting standing rule: "Always rebuild the graph after every extraction pass."
- 2026-09-01 (20:31): "scope filter silently dropping all 130 office docs (they convert to `.md` inside an excluded folder)" — two individually-correct stages composing into a hundred-document gap.
- 2026-09-01 (20:31): a related variant, "zero-yield files marked 'done' so they'd never retry (221 requeued)" — a success marker applied to work that produced nothing.
- 2026-08-31: the `com.keystone.dailybackup` failure traced to "3 project folders missing from the manifest," surfaced as `backup-error` with per-folder log entries rather than any execution failure.
- 2026-09-01 (20:33): "Every new `~/DEV/<folder>` breaks the backup until added to the manifest — default-deny working as intended; it caught a newly created folder within a minute."

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

## Evidence

# Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology

On 2026-05-21, a structured 7-day retrospective (covering May 14–21) and a cold-project triage exercise were conducted to address project sprawl across many concurrent initiatives. The retrospective produced a structured cross-project summary of work completed and 7 open loops with next actions; the triage sorted cold projects into 4 buckets and shipped a decision-tracking HTML artifact at `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html`.

## Key Points

- **7-day retrospective format:** a structured recap of all projects touched in a rolling window, categorized by status, covering CLI development (Zotero, Catapult), 5 new skills installed, Fireflies setup, memory and Obsidian integration, token dashboard setup, and side fixes for May 14–21. Concluded with 7 identified open loops, each paired with a concrete next action.
- **Cold-project 4-bucket triage:** cold projects (not touched during the retrospective window) are sorted into: **Resume** (active work, blocked on a specific next action), **Decide** (uncertain whether to continue; needs a deliberate go/no-go decision), **Done** (formally closeable), **Archive/Kill** (permanently deprioritized or abandoned). The 2026-05-21 run sorted 16 projects: 3 resume, 2 decide, 3 done, 8 archive/kill.
- **Triage output artifact:** `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html` — a self-contained HTML file summarizing all bucketed projects with statuses and next actions, usable offline without re-running the triage.
- **Hottest cold project:** `Risk_Stratification_Engine` was flagged as the highest-priority cold project to resume next.
- **Project sprawl as a recurring pattern:** the user explicitly noted difficulty maintaining orientation across many concurrent initiatives; periodic retrospectives and triage dashboards were identified as the structural remedy.

## Details

The retrospective was triggered by the user explicitly losing track of what had been started, stopped, or left mid-flight — a common failure mode when many parallel workstreams run simultaneously across different tools, repositories, and roles. Rather than relying on memory or ad-hoc review, the session generated a structured cross-project summary covering the prior 7 days, making the "what exists and where it stands" question answerable in a single, deliberate pass. The format mirrors a lightweight sprint retrospective: scope (what was touched), status (done vs. in-flight vs. blocked), and open loops (concrete next actions, not vague intentions).

The 4-bucket triage model is designed to force explicit decisions rather than letting cold projects accumulate indefinitely in an ambiguous "maybe later" state. **Resume** identifies projects with a clear next action that are still worth pursuing. **Decide** surfaces projects that need a deliberate go/no-go call rather than being quietly ignored — the act of naming these forces a decision that passive neglect defers indefinitely. **Done** provides a formal closure signal for work that is genuinely complete but hasn't been officially closed. **Archive/Kill** handles deliberate deprioritization — not forgotten, but explicitly moved out of active consideration. The HTML artifact makes the triage durable and reviewable without accessing the session that produced it; sharing it as a file also separates the "what was triaged" question from the "what should I do next" question, allowing the artifact to be reviewed asynchronously.

The retrospective also surfaced a secondary benefit: completing deferred follow-up work from prior sessions. Specifically, the Zotero CLI's `sync --full` verification — left pending after the v0.1 slash command was registered on 2026-05-19 — was completed during the retrospective, with 2,064 items ingested successfully in ~75 seconds. Catching and completing loose ends like this is a natural output of a structured retrospective: open loops that were "almost done" become clearly visible and easy to close within the retrospective session itself.

# Subagent-Driven Development (Two-Stage Review)

Subagent-Driven Development is a Claude Code skill/methodology for implementing tasks from a written plan via subagents, followed by two independent review passes - a spec-compliance review and a separate code-quality review - before a task is considered done. It was used on 2026-04-24 to complete the final task of the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]].

## Key Points

- Tasks are drawn from a written plan document (e.g., `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-04-24-perch-weight-room-domain.md`), with each task implemented by a subagent.
- After implementation, a spec-compliance reviewer checks the result against the plan's stated requirements using a checklist; Task 9 passed this stage 12/12.
- A second, separately-focused code-quality reviewer then reviews the same implementation for correctness and quality issues independent of the spec checklist.
- On Task 9, the code-quality reviewer caught a real bug - two chart-cleanup arrays in `report.html.j2` missing a `"trend-wr"` entry - that had passed both the implementer's self-review and the spec-compliance review.
- After the implementer fixed the flagged bug, the code-quality reviewer re-reviewed and passed it, completing the task.

## Details

The methodology separates "did this match the plan?" from "is this code actually correct and well-written?" into two distinct review passes, each performed independently. This separation matters because a fully spec-compliant implementation can still contain bugs that the spec's acceptance checklist simply doesn't enumerate - in this case, the plan's requirements for Task 9 didn't explicitly call out every chart-cleanup array that needed a `"trend-wr"` entry, so the spec-compliance reviewer had nothing to flag even though it checked all 12 of its listed items. The code-quality reviewer, working from a different lens (general code correctness rather than a fixed checklist), caught the omission.

This two-stage structure is a development-process instance of a broader pattern also seen in data-pipeline work: a single review/verification pass, however thorough by its own criteria, can miss errors that a differently-focused second pass would catch. See [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]] for how this Task 9 experience parallels an earlier citation-verification fix in [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]]. Practically, the methodology produced a clean outcome for the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]]: with Task 9's bug fixed and re-reviewed, the full 9-task feature reached 26/26 passing tests across 11 commits.

# "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" Deck Series (Education_Content_Agent)

The "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" series is a set of short educational decks for Baylor Applied Performance, generated programmatically by the `Education_Content_Agent` project. On 2026-08-19, three alternative visual directions were built as samples, the user selected the "split field" direction, and all five topic decks were rebuilt in it. The selected direction was written into `build-all.js` as the default so a later rebuild cannot silently revert to the prior editorial look.

## Key Points

- **Three directions were built as real samples, not descriptions:** A — *sequence rail* (a five-step argument along the top, current step lit); B — *split field* (a hard vertical divide, claim on dark green and evidence on bone, both visible at once); C — *annotated evidence* (numbered figure plus caption, paper-style). B was recommended and chosen.
- **The chosen direction became the code default.** `build-all.js` now defaults to split field, with `--direction annotated | sequence-rail | editorial` retained as opt-in flags. The stated rationale was explicitly about future-proofing: a rebuild six months later must not quietly produce the old design.
- **Prior versions were preserved, not overwritten.** The user declined the OneDrive overwrite; `5slides5minutes/` on OneDrive was left untouched at 10 decks (5 new topics in the previous design plus ACWR, CMJ, GPS, HRV, VBT), and the previous-design decks were pulled back down to `decks-out/previous-editorial-design/` so they exist in two places rather than only on a synced drive.
- **A PowerPoint-free renderer was built** that reads `.pptx` directly, after PowerPoint automation broke following a force-quit. Its text spacing is approximate in preview; the `.pptx` files themselves remain exact.
- **Layouts authored for full-width slides break in narrow columns.** The two-card comparison layout in the Post-Practice deck had headings wrapping into body text under the split field's narrower column; the fix was to stack the cards when the column is tight.

## Details

The session's structure — build three fully realized directions, view them side by side, then commit one — treats visual direction as a decision to be made against rendered artifacts rather than against prose descriptions. The three samples plus a `compare.html` contact sheet live in `decks-out/variants/`, which means the rejected directions remain inspectable rather than being discarded with the decision. This matters because the three directions encode genuinely different rhetorical structures: the sequence rail foregrounds a stepwise argument, the annotated-evidence direction foregrounds the figure as the primary object, and the split field holds claim and evidence in simultaneous view. Choosing among them is a choice about how the five-minute talk argues, not merely how it looks.

Encoding the chosen direction as the `build-all.js` default is the durability half of the decision. A generated-artifact pipeline whose visual direction lives only in the invocation flags will regress to whatever the code's default happens to be the next time someone runs a rebuild without remembering the flag — and the person running it six months out may not know a choice was ever made. Writing the selection into the default converts an undocumented convention into a property of the build, while the `--direction` flags keep the alternatives reachable. The parallel preservation decision applies the same reasoning to outputs: rather than overwriting the OneDrive copies, the previous-design decks were pulled back down into a named local archive folder, so the prior versions survive in a second location that does not depend on a synced cloud drive remaining intact.

The split field's narrower content column exposed a latent assumption in the deck layouts. The two-card comparison layout in the Post-Practice deck had been authored against a full-width slide and, once constrained, produced headings that wrapped into their own body text. The general lesson is that layouts inherit an unstated width assumption from the design they were first authored under, and a design-direction change is effectively a viewport change for every layout in the corpus — the same class of defect as slide charts that overflow only at short landscape viewports in [[concepts/athlete-monitoring-rtp-presentation]]. The fix, stacking the cards when the column is tight, is a responsive rule rather than a per-slide patch.

# Layouts Inherit an Unstated Width Assumption From the Design They Were Authored Under

Every slide or page layout carries an implicit assumption about the width it will be rendered into, fixed at the moment it was authored and never written down. Changing the surrounding design direction — as the 2026-08-19 move to a split-field deck design did — is functionally a viewport change applied to every layout in the corpus at once, and it surfaces those assumptions as breakage. The Post-Practice deck's two-card comparison layout, authored against a full-width slide, produced headings wrapping into their own body text once constrained to the split field's narrower content column.

## Key Points

- **The assumption is invisible until violated.** A layout that has only ever rendered at one width looks correct and states nothing about its width requirement; nothing in the artifact records that it was authored full-width.
- **A design-direction change is a bulk viewport change.** Adopting the split field narrowed the content column for every deck simultaneously, so a single design decision exercised every layout against a width none had been tested at.
- **The correct fix is a responsive rule, not a per-slide patch.** Stacking the two cards when the column is tight generalizes to any future narrow context; hand-adjusting the one broken slide would leave the assumption intact.
- **The same defect class recurs at non-default viewports.** The slide-8 chart overflow in the RTP conference deck appeared only at short landscape sizes (~896×414) and was fixed with `aspect-ratio` plus a `max-height` cap — a layout bug invisible at the default render size.
- **Automated collision checks do not cover this.** Text overflowing its own container leaves the container's geometry unchanged, so a box-versus-box gate reports the slide as clean.

## Details

What makes this failure class expensive is that the assumption and the breakage are separated by a decision no one associates with layout. The person choosing a visual direction is making a rhetorical and aesthetic choice — claim and evidence in simultaneous view, versus a stepwise rail, versus an annotated figure — and is not consciously altering the render width of every existing slide. Yet the width change is the mechanical consequence, and it lands on layouts authored months earlier by someone who had no reason to record what width they assumed. The practical implication is that any global design change should be treated as a re-verification event for the whole corpus rather than as a restyle of the frame around unchanged content.

The verification side is where this connects to a known gap in automated checking. The 2026-08-19 QA gate detected box-versus-box collisions reliably, but text spilling past its own container's bounds does not move that container, so the gate saw nothing wrong with the very slide that had broken — the precise blind spot documented in [[concepts/automated-layout-qa-gate]]. Compounding this, the preview available in that session came from a PowerPoint-free renderer whose text spacing is approximate, which is the wrong instrument for adjudicating whether text fits its box. The defect therefore had to be caught by human inspection of a rendered artifact, and it was found in the same session only because the direction change forced a full visual review. The generalizable practice is the one arrived at independently in the RTP deck work: render at more than one viewport, and treat the default size as insufficient evidence that a layout holds.
